content: I was trying to guess the name of docs#MonoidHom.map_mclosure, thinking it'd be called something like Submonoid.map_closure or Submonoid.closure_image but I couldn't figure it out and had to search it up. Why is this in the MonoidHom namespace?

Dot notation because it existed before the hom classes (I'm pretty sure). Also, since docs#Submonoid.map should be refactored to only accept a docs#MonoidHom, we'll be able to use dot notation again in the future.

But none of the definitions referenced in the signature of the theorem are in namespace MonoidHom, we have docs#Submonoid.map, docs#Submonoid.closure, and docs#Set.image. I think docs#Submodule.span_image does this more sensibly, it's in namespace Submodule and it references definitions in namespace Submodule in its statement (docs#Submodule.span, docs#Submodule.map), it wouldn't make sense to call this LinearMap.span_image.
Right, but it would have docs#MonoidHom in the type signature (and I think it used to long ago) if we fix docs#Submonoid.map
That's not to say your argument is meritless. I think I have tripped myself up looking for this too for the same reason.

From the Lean 3 PR https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib3/pull/14997 :

"This PR generalizes part of the basic API of monoid homs to monoid_hom_class. This notably includes things like monoid_hom.mker, submonoid.map and submonoid.comap. I left the namespaces unchanged, for example monoid_hom.mker remains the same even though it is now defined for any monoid_hom_class morphism; this way dot notation still (mostly) works for actual monoid homs."
yes but this doesn't explain why it's in the monoid_hom namespace to begin with
I thought it would be in the submonoid namespace
Dot notation is the entirety of the answer I think.
